title: How Two Teachers Brought the Science of Learning to their District
author: Kerry Cusick
summary: Kerry Cusick describes how she and a colleague turned a school PD presentation into an eighteen-hour in-district workshop on the science of learning for K-6 educators. They deliberately tied cognitive load, attention, memory and retrieval practice to earlier district work on engagement and UDL so it would not read as a fad. The course used six two-hour sessions with independent application tasks and a rose, bud and thorn reflection. Participants shared student work and enthusiasm, and colleagues asked for a second round. This is a modest implementation narrative of teacher-led professional development rather than a research argument, and it offers a practical template for grassroots PD.
points: Teacher-led in-house PD works when it connects new science to what colleagues already know and avoids looking like a trend.
The course was structured as six two-hour sessions plus independent assignments to earn in-service credit.
Linking learning science to prior district initiatives on engagement and UDL gave participants familiar touchpoints.
Application tasks and reflections kept participants using the content with their own students between sessions.
Demand for a Part 2 indicates teacher appetite for practical learning science when presented collegially.
quotes: In-house professional development is very much valued in our district, but the time to commit to it is often the barrier. Tara and I knew that this could be a successful workshop, but we didn’t want it to come across as a fad or a trend. We knew the science of learning was grounded in research, but we had to teach our participants this in a way where they could make connections to what they were already doing and activate prior knowledge.

Our 18 hour class was broken up into six 2 hour sessions, plus six hours of independent work to receive inservice credit or PDP’s. Our participants were 32 K-6 educators, ranging from Classroom Teachers, Special Educators, Speech and Language Pathologists, and Multilingual teachers. Our regional district has six elementary schools, and we had at least one participant from each of them.

This was our first go at sharing our passions about learning science and feeding others what we thought would enhance their teaching practices. This was where it got fun but also messy - we wanted to share the nuts and bolts about the science of learning but also knew that providing our participants with the knowledge to approach activities with the students in front of them was essential.

We wanted to have touchpoints so there could be a connection to previous knowledge. Therefore, the topics that we shared could be built on one another but also then applied to new approaches educators could use with their students.

Application by our participants was a key piece of our workshop. After each face-to-face session, they completed independent assignments ranging from reading articles, listening to podcasts, watching videos, composing poems, completing activities with their students, and a rose, bud, and thorn reflection.

I would get emails and texts from our participants raving about the podcasts. They also sent photos showcasing student work. Braindumps, hexagonal thinking activities connecting to content, and engaging activities and games to highlight retrieval practices - oh my!

We hope that the district will continue to build on what Tara and I started. Many colleagues have asked for a Part 2! We learned so much, and our colleagues started to bring it back to our students. Throughout this process, we kept saying “If only we knew this when we were first starting out in our careers…
